I really enjoy walking around Sants station. It's a huge complex with countless tracks running through its underground interior like arteries from its heart.

Despite being modernized, it retains the old display of train schedules and platforms, those where a wooden plaque rotates around a central axis until the desired character appears.

One looks at the panel somewhat like looking at a lottery, waiting for the letters to form (which, incidentally, don’t do so in order), hoping their train moves up the list and doesn’t end up in the dreaded "delayed" state.

I usually don’t like large, crowded spaces, but the station is different. In the station, everyone has a purpose, pursuing their goal, and the most charming thing about the place: people are just passing through. That's the best part of the station, its people.

There’s always the couple saying goodbye, hugging for longer than reasonable, closing their eyes tightly, repeating the mantra in their heads about how much they’ll miss each other, how sad they feel, as if clicking their heels three times will make them comfortably seated on the couch like they were yesterday. As everyone knows, there's no place like home.

Another classic at the station are the people with large backpacks, dressed in scruffy clothes, always in a hurry, always running. They can be identified by their determined walk in one direction, only to abruptly change course because they’ve seen a revealing sign. They usually carry a crumpled ticket (usually bought online) in one hand and an inherited wheeled suitcase in the other. I like their spirit of improvisation, of having a plan but not minding if it changes at the last minute. Besides, they usually sit on the floor without any trouble and seem to have infinite patience, always waiting for the next train, and finding ways to entertain themselves with anything that falls into their hands to pass the time. A book, crosswords... They live in that primal simplicity where as long as there’s water in the backpack and a bathroom nearby, everything will be fine. Why would anyone need anything more?

In contrast, we have the big executives in expensive suits who walk around with the self-sufficiency of someone who has everything under control. They don’t bump into people because they know where they’re going, they fix their gaze and head unerringly toward their goal, like it or not. If you happen to be in their way... “you’d better move aside, kid. I don’t have time to waste.”

I like these people too. Especially when they end up sitting in McDonald’s with their jacket hanging on the chair, tie over their shoulder, a paper napkin tucked into their shirt, devouring a sandwich dripping onto the table. You can see that childhood gleam in their eyes because, let’s not kid ourselves, they’re probably used to caviar, but a hamburger is always a hamburger. They taste the same as when you were a kid.

They drop their mask, abandon the pose, and at lunchtime, they become equal to our backpacking friends sitting on the floor, eating exactly the same sandwich. McDonald’s makes us all equal, to say something good about the franchise.

It’s only temporary, let’s not kid ourselves, when they put on their jacket again, it’s like a warrior donning chain mail once more. That armor is thick, and the pose returns in full force. Everyone goes on with their lives, and all is well. And that’s how it should be.

Finally, one of the common features of all train stations is the number of strange and unique people you encounter. Given the current times, they’re often avoided and looked at with incriminating eyes. Somewhere between a vagabond and a delinquent, it’s easy to find elderly women pushing supermarket carts filled with the most varied junk, strange men playing a four-string guitar in a corner, someone impeccably dressed with a stately bearing and slicked-back hair but barefoot, not to mention the variety of outlandish hats.

They don’t seem to be coming from or going anywhere; it’s like the native life of the small ecosystem of the station.

Sometimes they look up when the loudspeaker announces departures, listening intently. Maybe they’re waiting for their train to be announced at last. Maybe they’re waiting to hear the arrival of the one they’ve been waiting for so long. I like going home thinking they’ll finally find what they’re looking for.
